Context

FlowCast is product 12 of 12 in the marketplace-app portfolio: a Xero App Store app giving SMB owners a 13-week cash forecast with traffic lights, what-if scenario sliders, invoice-chasing nudges, bank-feed anomaly alerts, and an accountant portal that triages a whole client book reds-first.

It has been built entirely in a sandbox under D13 (100% automated coverage, zero pragmas) across 36 workbook versions and 24 tracker versions between 5 and 20 September 2026, with two independent external AI reviews (ChatGPT V001 on 13 Sep, Perplexity V001 on 16 Sep). Neither the code nor any document has ever touched a real Xero organisation.

This document exists because the same fact has to be said two ways at once: the engineering discipline is unusually strong (49 suites / 719 tests at 100%, 14 gate files proved by 15 mutations), and the product is further from a listing than a "77 of 100 stories Done" rollup suggests. Both are true, and the second is the one a reader needs.

Colour convention throughout: green = built, tested at 100% and gate-proved in the sandbox; amber = code-complete but never run live or waiting on a decision; red = not built; grey = outside the codebase (Xero, vendors, people).

How to use this document

  • Read the four diagrams first (sections 1–4); each has a one-paragraph reading guide under it. They are also supplied as standalone PNG and SVG files so they can be pasted into a deck or printed.
  • Section 5 is the feature-by-feature and story-by-story record: what "Done" means for each, and the exact reason anything is not Done. Every reason names its source id (a finding, decision, risk or handover item) so it can be checked in tracker v024 or workbook v036.
  • Section 6 is the version timeline — one line per release, what it did and why. The companion Excel workbook (versiondetail_manualtest) carries the same versions in full with manual test cases per version.
  • When a status changes, do not edit this version: raise v002 with the change in Version Control. Nothing here is deleted between versions; superseded lines are marked.
  • Vocabulary: "Done" = code + 100% automated tests + a gate that fails under the original defect. "Code-complete — pending live" = the same, but the story can only be proved against a live Xero org. "Drafted" = a document that exists and has not been published or reviewed. "Not started" = nothing exists.

1. What FlowCast is

FlowCast answers two questions for a small business on Xero — "will I run out of cash in the next 13 weeks?" and "who owes me, and what happens if I chase them?" — and lets an accountant answer them for every client at once. It reads the organisation's Xero data (bank balances, sales invoices, supplier bills, repeating invoices, bank feed), computes a week-by-week cash position with traffic lights, lets the owner try what-if scenarios, plans invoice-chasing nudges, and watches the bank feed for anomalies.

2. How it works — the live data path

The architecture as it exists in code v0.30.0, laid out along the path data takes; every box names its source file. The path from Xero to the forecast routes and the scheduler is new in sprint E6 (20 Sep 2026) — before it, the forecast engine was a pure function fed by demo fixtures (Perplexity BLOCKER PPX-01).

3.2 The gates (14 files, 15 mutation proofs)

Coverage proves a module executes; it never proves anything calls it. Each gate fails the build when a specific shipped defect is reintroduced, and prove-gates.js demonstrates that by reintroducing the real defect into real source. This is the strongest evidence in the package and the reason "Done" can be trusted at all.

GateRuleDefect it exists to catch
reachabilityGateEvery src export — and since E6 every public class method — has a production caller; file-level pardons gone; KNOWN_GAPS expireINT-F1/F2, F3-02, GAP-F2, PPX-01 (HOLE-4)
publishedClaimsGateEvery customer promise in docs/ is backed by code (and a driver, for policies)INT-F2, GAP-F2, INT-F5
tenantIsolationGateNo shared state across a per-tenant loopF4-01
docFreshnessGateOutsider-facing documents acknowledge every moduleREV-1 (L-F14)
asyncOwnershipGateEvery un-awaited promise has an ownerCHAOS-1
supplyChainGateSBOM matches the lockfile; no secret-shaped literals; security headers on every response; no stale published claimsFC-R015, FC-R006, FC-R002
migrationSafetyGateMigrations are additive (expand/contract)OPS-1
environmentReview (fail-closed boot)Production refuses to start without DATABASE_URL / FLOWCAST_DATA_KEYE5b-01/02
dataPathGate (E6)Each headline feature reachable from a route or tick with no fixture on the chain; the engine's caller itself live-fedPPX-01 — caught BROKEN on first proof, strengthened
invoiceTypeGate (E6)Every /Invoices query typed; mapper asserts per rowPPX-02
currencyGate (E6)Amounts reach the engine only via toBaseCurrency; provenance on every recordPPX-06
platformLimitsGate (E6)Each documented Xero limit enforced on the live call; daily default = StarterPPX-04/05
platformDriftGate (E6)Platform assumptions sourced, dated, within budget; contradicted ones ownedPPX-03
forecastRealismGate (E6)No live-path payProbability literal; receivables via the calibratorPPX-08

v0232026-09-13 11:20TENANT-ISOLATION GATE built and wired into CI — third portable gate, written because F4-01 proved L-F5 (knowing a defect class does not stop you writing it). Rule: inside a loop over tenants, a variable declared OUTSIDE the loop may not be both assigned and read within the body — that is tenant N deciding tenant N+1 behaviour. Pure accumulators (count += 1, arr.push) exempt as write-only. THE GATE WAS BROKEN TWICE BEFORE IT WORKED, and that is the report: run against the real scheduler.ts with F4-01 reintroduced it PASSED twice — (1) read-detection stripped whole assignment statements, erasing the self-referential x = f(x) carry which is precisely the shape it exists to catch; (2) loop offsets used source.indexOf(line), which returns the FIRST match, and scheduler.ts has three identical tenant-loop headers so two loops were never analysed at all. Both fixed; only then does the reintroduced defect fail the gate, naming the leaked variable. 29 suites / 394 tests at 100% zero pragmas; three gates now green and named individually in CI. Lesson L-F6: a broken static gate does not complain, it approves — the fixture test passed from the first run while the gate was blind

HOLE-2 claims gate: gutting the encryption call (the INT-F2 defect) left the gate GREEN because import { encryptField } matched the claim pattern while the storage path stored plaintext. Fixed the same way; re-proved to fail with claim id, document and customer impact. Known limits documented rather than hidden: dead clusters flagged at the root not per member; file-level ENTRY_POINTS pardon every export in that module (the first probe proved nothing because it ran in an exempt file); all three gates are text lints not AST analysis. 29 suites / 395 tests at 100% zero pragmas; all three gates now proved against reintroduced real defects. v0252026-09-13 11:58PORTABLE GATE PACK + PROOF HARNESS (gates/prove-gates.js, npm run prove:gates, now in CI). Addresses the portfolio open item "port gates to the other products", which L-F7 made dangerous rather than merely pending: a ported gate arrives GREEN, and green means nothing — four of the gates built here were silently permissive on their first green run. For each gate the harness takes a REAL source file, applies a mutation reintroducing the REAL defect that gate exists to catch (INT-F1 unwire recordNudge, INT-F2 gut encryption, F4-01 shared PollState), runs the gate and REQUIRES IT TO FAIL, always restoring the file; non-zero exit if any gate stays green under its own defect. All three currently PROVED. The harness is META-PROVED: reintroducing HOLE-1 makes it report BROKEN and exit 1. It also reports STALE when a mutation anchor no longer exists, so a silently non-applying mutation cannot pass quietly. gates/README.md carries porting steps — empty every exemption list first (expect 15-40 first-run hits), write mutations from defects that ACTUALLY happened in that product (an invented mutation re-tests the author assumptions, the trap the fixtures fell into), and DO NOT wire a gate into CI until the harness prints PROVED. Honest limits documented: text lints not AST, dead clusters flagged at root, file-level exemptions coarse. 29 suites / 395 tests at 100% zero pragmas. Lesson L-F8

Every release would have dropped all tokens (forcing every tenant to reinstall), reset usage counters (fresh 50 nudges — undoing F-005/INT-F1), cleared nudge history (re-chasing every customer — undoing F-006), reset dunning counters (undoing F4-02), and lost deletion schedules (the published 30-day policy never firing — undoing F-007/GAP-F2). The reachability gate failed the build TWICE on code from this same sitting — the layer was unwired from boot (the INT-F1 shape, caught in minutes not sittings), and closePool had no caller which surfaced that graceful shutdown did not exist. Restart-survival proof: two app instances over one store — the second still reports 50 used, still refuses the 51st, still holds the history. 30 suites / 433 tests at 100% zero pragmas; gates still proved. v0282026-09-13 16:38ENVIRONMENT-ASSUMPTIONS REVIEW (acting on L-F10: what does this code believe about the world that no test asserts?). 3 findings, all broken by the deploy model this codebase already ships. ENV-1 CRITICAL: startScheduler assumed EXACTLY ONE PROCESS. Blue/green runs BOTH colours during a switch and scaling runs N — so every overdue customer received N NUDGES THE SAME DAY (the duplicate chasing F-006 exists to prevent, reintroduced by deployment not logic), plus N dunning emails, N bank polls against the 5,000/day budget, and N purge runs racing the same rows. Fixed with a Postgres advisory lock, re-checked per tick so a follower promotes itself when the leader dies. ENV-2 CRITICAL: accepted webhook events sat in memory, but fast-ack tells Xero 200 and Xero NEVER redelivers — a restart between ack and drain destroyed them permanently and silently, the exact failure the redelivery-heals design was built to avoid. Now persisted before the ACK with boot recovery and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED draining; the ingest buffer has no FK by design so deleteTenant clears it explicitly, else the 30-day policy leaks through it. ENV-3 Major: business hours were documented local but computed in UTC — the published 4-business-hour SLA was simply wrong for any non-UTC desk (an India team had deadlines against a day ending 22:30 local). utcOffsetMinutes now explicit; DST deliberately out of scope as OBS-003. /health now reports durableStore AND singleWriter so operators see what is actually guaranteed. OBS-004 logged not fixed: webhook-driven rate limiting stays per-process (needs a decision on per-call round-trip cost). 31 suites / 453 tests at 100% zero pragmas; gates still proved. Lesson L-F11
v0292026-09-13 16:47OPS-ARTIFACT REVIEW — applying the L-F11 method (read one artifact against another) to the operational artifacts vs the database that only started existing two releases ago. OPS-1 CRITICAL: THE DEPLOY PIPELINE NEVER RAN MIGRATIONS — any release adding one would deploy code whose queries hit tables that do not exist. OPS-3 CRITICAL: /health answers from MEMORY and that is what gated the switch, so a slot with a wrong/unreachable/unmigrated DATABASE_URL reported ok:true, passed verify-slot.sh and would have been handed live traffic. The two COMPOUND: OPS-1 breaks the slot, OPS-3 certifies it anyway. Fixed: migrations run before the slot starts; new /ready probes the store and verify-slot.sh requires it. OPS-2 Major: blue/green runs TWO releases against ONE database and rollback re-points to the old colour AFTER the new schema is applied — nothing enforced that schema changes were safe for a still-running previous release. Fourth gate added (migrationSafetyGate): migrations may only ADD, removals are a separate later release citing the release that dropped the last reader; the runbook now states the rollback contract explicitly instead of implying it. Lesson L-F12
v0302026-09-13 16:52CHAOS REVIEW — re-running the L-F12 pairing against the newest subsystem: the degradation artifacts were written when XERO WAS THE ONLY DEPENDENCY, and Postgres has been in every request path for three releases. CHAOS-1 CRITICAL: two void-promise calls sat on the database path, one on the WEBHOOK FAST-ACK ROUTE. Since Node 15 an unhandled rejection TERMINATES THE PROCESS — verified on this runtime (node v22) with a three-line script: the process died. A transient Postgres error during ordinary webhook traffic would not have degraded FlowCast, it would have KILLED it, on every instance sharing that database simultaneously (both blue/green colours), leaving the router nothing to fall back to. Fixed: both sites run through safely() which counts and reports but always resolves; process guards report unhandled rejections while the service continues and drain deliberately on uncaught exceptions; 3+ clustered failures surface as store:degraded on /ready. Pinned by a test sending a signed webhook to a store that fails every write — the route still returns 200 empty, the event is held, the failure counted. CHAOS-2 Major: the chaos runbook only knew about Xero; extended with a database-outage drill stating expected behaviour per path, every row backed by a test rather than an intention. 35 suites / 478 tests at 100% zero pragmas; two defensive-unreachable fallbacks removed rather than pragma-suppressed; gates still proved; live boot ready:true. Lesson L-F13: void promise is the quietest way to write a crash

Caught mistake recorded honestly: the rewritten review pack first claimed 494 tests when the real number was 482 — a figure written from memory into a document whose whole purpose is to be trusted by an outsider; corrected to a form that cannot go stale. 35 suites / 485 tests at 100% zero pragmas; gates proved. Lesson L-F14
v0322026-09-13 17:29DOC-FRESHNESS GATE (fifth gate) — closing L-F14 mechanically. That lesson ended with three claims gate-enforced and "the rest rely on someone looking", which is exactly what failed: the reviewer pack went 13 releases out of date on the critical path because nobody inside needs to read it. Rule: a document written for an OUTSIDER must acknowledge the parts of the system it claims to describe — if a module exists and its map has never heard of it, the build fails, so a subsystem cannot ship without the reviewer and pen-tester maps being updated in the same change. Each covered document records its AUDIENCE in the gate, so a failure names who is affected. Exemptions are per-module with reasons; "later/todo/tbd/for now" fails because that phrasing IS the decay. IT FIRED ON FIRST RUN, on documents rewritten six minutes earlier: the v031 rewrite added the eight newest subsystems but silently omitted the original feature modules, and the security pack described "the database" in prose without ever naming db or pg. Both completed — per-module what-to-challenge tables and a vendor module map to scope against by name. The harness then caught a WEAK MUTATION not a weak gate: the first proof deleted one of two leaderLock mentions and the gate rightly stayed green; re-pointed at a module mentioned once, it fails as intended. 36 suites / 492 tests at 100% zero pragmas; five gates in CI, four provable ones all PROVED. Lesson L-F15
v0332026-09-13 18:48ASYNC-OWNERSHIP GATE (sixth, and the last derived from a shipped defect) + REVIEW PLAYBOOK. A real defect found first: the worker tick called drainOnce with no catch, and drainOnce RETHROWS after re-queuing (F4-04) — so every store or sink failure produced an unhandled rejection that the degradation counter never saw and /ready never showed. The process guards stopped it being fatal, but it was invisible. Both that and the SIGTERM shutdown call now have owners; shutdown failures are reported with credentials redacted. Sixth gate: a promise started and not awaited must have an owner (safely(), or an explicit .catch). Only resilience.ts is exempt — it IS the owner of last resort and cannot wrap itself. Proved against the exact CHAOS-1 shape; all five provable gates now print PROVED. REVIEW PLAYBOOK written (gates/REVIEW_PLAYBOOK.md): the eight review passes in the order that proved productive — cold review by module, external verification sweep, artifact-gap audit, integration audit, review-the-previous-session, environment assumptions, artifact pairing, outsider-first document review — plus the rules learned the hard way and how to run them on another product. ~40 defects were found in code that was already at 100% coverage with zero backlog; the gates catch recurrence, the passes find what nobody has thought of yet. 36 suites / 500 tests at 100% zero pragmas; six gates in CI. Recommendation recorded: this is a natural stopping point for sandbox work

7. Glossary

TermMeaning
D13Portfolio rule: 100% automated coverage on all four metrics, zero pragmas; discovery interviews parked.
GateA test that fails the build when a specific class of shipped defect is reintroduced; "proved" means prove-gates.js reintroduced the real defect and the gate failed.
Enhancement poolA second point pool (D-F7) for corrective work arising from reviews, so the 399-point story baseline is never inflated by fixes.
PPX-nn / FC-RnnnFindings from the Perplexity V001 / ChatGPT V001 external reviews.
E6-FnFindings made during sprint E6 (20 Sep 2026) by Claude while executing the Perplexity response.
KNOWN_GAPA reachability-gate exemption that names a RAID risk and an expiry date; the build fails when the date passes.
Live sweepThe 12-step scripted verification against a real Xero dev org (docs/live-sweep/verification-sweep.md). Not yet run.
XASSXero App Store Subscriptions — in-store billing, deprecated by Xero effective March 2026.

Not claimed anywhere in this document: enterprise-grade, production-ready, market-ready, or that any green item has been proved against a live Xero organisation. "Done" is a sandbox word until the live sweep runs.
